intro.summary: Create a window, clear its back buffer with Direct3D 12, and present your first frame.
overview.heading: When to use Direct3D 12
overview.purpose: Direct3D 12 is Microsoft's low-level graphics API. It's suited to engines and games that need direct control over the GPU. Your app records command lists, tracks resource states, and manages synchronization.
overview.choice: Choose Direct3D 12 for a Windows project if you need explicit GPU control similar to Vulkan or want LIMEN's optional DLSS and FSR modules. It gives you more control over how a frame executes than OpenGL or Direct3D 11 and takes more code to set up.
requirements.heading: 1. Set up the project
requirements.folder: In the LIMEN source directory, create a folder named first-d3d12. Save the next section's code as Main.hx inside it.
requirements.paragraph: You need 64-bit Windows and a GPU that supports Direct3D 12. Follow the LIMEN installation guide and copy limen.hdll, d3d12.limen, dxcompiler.dll, and dxil.dll from the build output into the app directory. Use source files and native modules from the same LIMEN version.
program.heading: 2. Render your first frame
program.intro: Record a back-buffer clear in a command list. Submit the list to the queue and present the frame. A fence lets you wait for the GPU to finish.
run.heading: 3. Build, run, and experiment
run.runtime: Run the commands from the directory containing Main.hx. If you use the bundled Windows runtime, copy hl.exe and libhl.dll from the build output into that directory and run .\hl.exe main.hl.
run.result: A window with a blue background should open. Close it, change the color or title in Main.hx, and run both commands again.
